verdicts.why: B cuts harder: two afftdn passes at nr=30, a 10 kHz lowpass and ten notches up to 300 Hz. That drops its fidelity to 0.786, below the raw input's 0.841, which suggests the underwater sound the client asked to avoid. It also adds synthetic pink noise and shifts timing with an extra 0.05 s start trim. A's gentler chain improves fidelity to 0.868 and removes more hum (0.7 vs 3.0 dB). A's one failed check is levels_evened: it narrowed the dip gap from -8.4 to -4.4 dB against B's -2.3, and that shortfall is smaller than B's damage to the voice.

A passes all 10 checks. Its dip gap closes to -2.3 dB, while B only reaches -4.4 dB and fails levels_evened, so B misses the brief's explicit request to bring the quiet drift passages up to match. A pays for this with heavier processing: two afftdn passes at nr=30, a 10 kHz low-pass, a gate and added pink noise drop its fidelity to 0.786, against B's 0.868, which is a real risk of the 'underwater' sound. B is the gentler and more natural-sounding script with better hum removal, but a missed brief item outweighs that, so A wins only slightly.

B sets the music level from the measured loudness of both files and ducks with a gain curve built from silencedetect speech segments. That gives a deep 21 dB duck, a 22.5 dB voice-to-music ratio and higher voice fidelity (0.962), and the bed still comes back up in the pauses. A uses a fixed -20 dB bed cut and a ratio-6 sidechain compressor, which only ducks 9.4 dB. That falls short of 'well below the voice', and the hard-coded threshold and pre-gain only suit this particular music file. B's post-speech bump overlaps the fade-out, which is a small flaw, but it still ends cleanly about 4 s after the last word, so overall B is the better mix to ship.

A sets the music level from the measured loudness of both files and ducks it with a gain curve built from the detected speech segments. That gives a deep, deliberate duck (21.1 dB, 22.5 dB voice-over-music) that comes back in the pauses, plus the best voice fidelity (0.962) and a cleaner ending (-72 dB). B cuts the music by a fixed -20 dB that only suits this one file, and its 6:1 sidechain compressor ducks just 9.4 dB with a 500 ms release that may not recover in short pauses, so the words have less clear space and the bed is less 'well below' the voice.

A's sidechain compressor barely ducks the bed (5.5 dB). The music ends up louder than the voice (VMR -3.5 dB) and voice fidelity is poor (0.588), so it fails the ducks, voice_above_music and voice_intact checks. B sets the voice-to-music balance from measured loudness and uses a scripted duck curve that drops the bed 16 dB under each line and brings it back up between lines. It passes all 13 checks and fades the bed and sting out properly for a much cleaner ending (-59.7 vs -31.1 dB). B's silence-trimming and timeline logic is more complex, but it handles leading and trailing silence in the takes, while A's fixed music level and sidechain settings only work if the levels happen to line up.

B's music bed sits above the voice (vmr -3.5 dB) and ducks only 5.5 dB. Its sidechain compressor uses a ratio of 4 and never sets music level relative to voice loudness, so the voice is buried and voice fidelity drops to 0.588. It fails the ducks, voice_above_music and voice_intact checks. A trims each line, sets the music level from measured voice LUFS and draws an explicit 16 dB duck envelope with ramps around each line. It passes all 13 checks with a much quieter tail (-59.7 vs -31.1 dB).

verdicts.why: B passes all 10 checks. It hits -16.0 LUFS exactly by running a two-pass linear loudnorm, and its notch filters cut the hum prominence from 43.8 to 2.3 dB. A also hard-codes volume boosts at fixed timestamps (13.0-17.4 s and 28.3-32.2 s), which only works for this one file. A passes all 10 checks. It lands exactly on -16 LUFS with -1 dBTP, and its notch filters cut the hum from 43.8 dB to 2.3 dB above the floor, while B leaves the hum almost untouched (38.5 dB) because it has no notch filters. B also misses loudness by 2.8 LU, since it uses single-pass loudnorm with no measurement pass. On top of that, B boosts the two quiet passages using timestamps hard-coded for this one file, which is fragile, while A evens levels with dynaudnorm, which adapts to whatever file it gets. A is a bit further from the loudness target (-15.2 vs -15.9 LUFS) and uses a fixed 0.18 music gain, but both of those still meet the spec.

A also hard-codes the fade points and delays for these exact files, while B measures the line lengths, trims silence, works out the start times and sets the bed level from measured loudness, so B holds up better if the recordings change.
